title: Your end-to-end design project
idea: The mid-course project asks you to take one system from this chapter and design it yourself, from requirements to running code with checks.
points: Pick one system from this chapter, such as a parking lot, cache or logger.
Write numbered requirements first; each one becomes a check in plain Java.
Nouns become classes, verbs become methods, and changeable rules become interfaces.
Finish with concurrency and failure cases: who races, and what can go wrong.

hero.title: A checklist for any LLD project

items.label: 1. Scope
items.text: List five to eight numbered requirements. Write down what you will not build.

items.label: 2. Entities
items.text: Underline nouns as classes and verbs as methods. Choose `record`, `enum` or class.

items.label: 3. Relations
items.text: Draw a class diagram: is-a, has-a, and who owns whom.

items.label: 4. Contracts
items.text: Hide each changeable rule behind an `interface`. Name a pattern only if it fits.

items.label: 5. Risks
items.text: Mark shared state and pick a lock. List invalid inputs and their exceptions.

items.label: 6. Prove it
items.text: Turn each requirement into a named check, run it, and fix until all pass.

code.title: Requirements as checks
code.caption: Step 6 on a tiny parking lot: each numbered requirement is one named check.

walk.text: A hand-written `check` runner: no JUnit needed, and failures are counted.
R1: the happy path. A free spot hands back a ticket.
R2 and R3 are refusal rules; set up state so only one rule can apply.
R4 proves state is released, then a summary line reports the result.
`park` is `synchronized`: step 5 decided two gates may call it at once.

pitfalls: Do not start with classes; unclear scope makes every later choice a guess.
Do not force a pattern in; name one only when a rule really varies.
Write a check per requirement, and make each one fail for only one reason.

quiz.q: You have 45 minutes for the project. What should exist before your first class?
options: A thread-safe version of every method
Numbered requirements with a clear out-of-scope list
A class diagram showing every Gang of Four pattern
A complete set of JUnit 5 tests with Mockito
quiz.why: Requirements decide which classes, rules and checks you need. Without scope, code, diagrams and tests all chase guesses.

takeaway: Scope, entities, relations, contracts, risks, checks: in that order, every time.
